world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Rombo (romb1244) is not in the catalog. the list of works with stress in the title had one item, Philippson 1991 (thesis, open full text at DDL Lyon; copy now; Read in full text: Rombo ('chaga-est E 62c') is only inventoried in group XXI with a single + (limited data); all Chaga analysis (pp. 384-387, Annexe pp. 512-513) is for Vunjo, taken from McHugh 1990 — tone plus partially free lexical accent (penultimate of the theme for most themes) plus a demarcative length culmination — so it is a statement about another variety, silent on Rombo. The best first-hand statement on Rombo comes from material already held by the project from an earlier reading, verified here: Shinagawa 2021 (ILCAA, open access), p. 197 fn. 15, classifies Rombo as a tone language with weak accentual properties that fails Hyman's culminativity criterion, i.e. not a stress-accent language; no positional stress rule is given there, in Shinagawa 2014 (sketch sec. 1.4 p. 13) or in Philippson & Montlahuc 2003 (Mashati Rombo tone). Still unobtained: Montlahuc 2000 INALCO thesis on eastern Chaga (print only, not on HAL/theses.fr) and Shinagawa 2025 Oxford Guide chapter on Mkuu E623C (paywalled DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198808343.003.0070) — medium priority as possible first-hand accent statements for Rombo varieties. discovery went through on-disk copies, the DDL full-text server and theses.fr. updated (addendum).

new_statements.quote: この必須性と唯一性（culminativity：語は「最大ひとつの」音調上のプロミネンスを有する＝複数のプロミネンスを有さない）を同時に満たすものが、典型的なstress accent言語であるというのが同論文の提案であるが、それに従えばロンボ語は前者は満たす（あくまでも単独形でということだが）ものの後者は満たさないという点で、アクセント性の弱いトーン言語（同論文の定義では、ピッチが形態素の語彙的な実現に何らかの形で関与している言語）と位置付けられることになる。
new_statements.translation: That paper's [Hyman 2006] proposal is that a language which satisfies both this obligatoriness and culminativity (culminativity: a word has 'at most one' tonal prominence, i.e. does not have multiple prominences) is a typical stress-accent language; following it, Rombo satisfies the former (though only in isolation forms) but not the latter, and is therefore to be classed as a tone language with weak accentual properties (in that paper's definition, a language in which pitch is involved in some way in the lexical realization of morphemes).

Surrounding section is entirely about the four 2-syllable stem patterns (-ØØ/-Ø…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rombo is a tone language (privative H vs. unmarked, syllable as TBU, surface H / upstepped super-high / downstepped H / L). It is explicitly not a stress-accent language: every word carries at least one H in isolation (obligatoriness), but words may carry more than one H (no culminativity), so no single culminative word prominence and no positional stress rule is given. Nouns in isolation avoid all-L patterns; before an associative all noun H's are neutralised to L. Affirmative main-clause verbs get a H on the first or second syllable (verb-initial H, IH), absent in negatives and subordinates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the source describes multiple H tones per word, not stress levels.
new_statements.exceptions: Obligatoriness holds only in isolation forms; noun tone patterns show considerable free variation and neutralisation, especially among young speakers; verb stems sometimes behave as both H and L class; tone patterns are described as in progressive obscuring/simplification.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation (isolation) forms of nouns, plus phrase-level contexts (copula, negative ku, associative, possessive); the (non-)culminativity remark is about the word in isolation. Shinagawa 2014 sketch sec. 1.4 p. 13 adds only that Chaga languages in general are said to have complex tone (or accent) patterns, much obscured in present-day Rombo.
new_statements.identity_note: Shinagawa's Rombo data (2014 sketch, 2014 vocabulary, 2021 tone chapter) come from a variety he places on the Mkuu-Keni continuum of Rombo District (Maho E623C Mkuu / E623D Keni), i.e. South-Rombo in Philippson & Montlahuc's (2003) terms; Montlahuc's own Rombo research (reported second-hand in that chapter) is on the Mashati variety of North-Rombo, which lacks tone shift. Glottolog romb1244 covers Rombo as a whole; no separate glottocodes for these dialects were verified. McHugh 1987, listed by Glottolog under romb1244, is on Wunjo/Kivunjo (Central Chaga), not Rombo.

new_statements.translation: That paper [Hyman 2006] proposes that a language satisfying both obligatoriness and culminativity (a word has 'at most one' tonal prominence, i.e. no multiple prominences) is a typical stress-accent language; following it, Rombo satisfies the former (though only in isolation forms) but not the latter, and is therefore to be placed as a tone language with weak accentual properties (in that paper's definition, a language in which pitch is involved in some way in the lexical realization of morphemes).
new_statements.citation: Shinagawa, Daisuke. 2021. Rombo-go (Bantu E623) no seichō patān gaikan [An overview of the tone patterns of Rombo (Bantu E623)]. In Kaji, Shigeki (ed.), Afurika shogo no seichō, akusento [Tone and accent in African languages], ch. 9, pp. 177-208. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies (CC BY 4.0).
new_statements.reading: Rombo is a tone language (lexical H vs. toneless stems, with a 'PLH' prefix-H property and downstep/spreading), not a stress-accent language: words may carry more than one H prominence, so culminativity fails; obligatoriness holds only for isolation forms. No positional word-stress rule (penultimate or otherwise) is stated anywhere in the chapter, in Shinagawa's 2014 grammatical sketch (sec. 1.4, p. 13: all Chaga languages are said to have complex tone-or-accent patterns, much levelled in young speakers' Rombo), or in Philippson & Montlahuc 2003 (Mashati North-Rombo: SH/H/L contrast, no tone shift). Best coding for a stress catalog: tonal, no word stress reported (a phrase-final demarcative length culmination is attested for Chaga generally by Philippson 1991, but only for Vunjo).

tone_statements.citation: Mramba, Peter T. 2025. Uchunguzi wa Tabia za Toni katika Vitenzi Visoukomo Sahili na Nomino za silabi moja za Kirombo [An investigation of tonal behaviour in simple non-finite verbs and monosyllabic-stem nouns of Kirombo]. SAUT Multidisciplinary Journal of Education (SMJE) 4(1), March 2025, article pp. 1-25 (issue pp. 23-47). Mwanza/Morogoro: St. Augustine University of Tanzania.
tone_statements.quote: Aidha, Kirombo kinadhihirisha wazi kina toni kulingana na ruwaza za maneno yake ambayo kiothografia huonekana sawa ilhali wazawa wa lugha hiyo wanapoyatumia katika mazungumzo yao huchomoza maana tofauti. Tutazame mfano (1) hapa chini: 1. a) ílya ‘kula’ ilyá ‘kukataa’ b) íla ‘kulala’ ilá ‘kuita’ Hivyo, katika 1(a) tunaona mambo yafuatayo: tonijuu ikijitokeza katika silabi ya kwanza ya neno maana yake huwa ‘kula’ na maana hubadilika na kuwa ‘kukataa’ toni inapojitokeza katika silabi ya pili ya neno.
tone_statements.translation: Moreover, Kirombo clearly shows that it has tone, judging from word patterns that look identical in spelling but yield different meanings when native speakers use them in speech. Consider example (1): a) ílya 'to eat' / ilyá 'to refuse'; b) íla 'to sleep' / ilá 'to call'. Thus in 1(a) we see: when the high tone appears on the first syllable of the word the meaning is 'eat', and the meaning changes to 'refuse' when the tone appears on the second syllable of the word.
tone_statements.locator: article p. 2, sec. 2.0 'Lugha ya Kirombo', example (1); H/L definitions and H-as-basic-tone statement article pp. 6-7; JC conclusion for monosyllabic nouns article p. 23
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone, two tones H (J) vs L (C) with H treated as the underlying marked tone; contrast carried by H placement within the word (minimal pairs, also noun/verb pairs); monosyllabic-stem infinitives/nouns = H prefix + L stem; surface falling tone from glide formation; TBU = syllable; no stress claim.

tone_statements.citation: Julius, A. T. [Julius Alex Tarimo]. 2023. Linguistic variations among dialects of Kirombo. MA (Linguistics) dissertation, The University of Dodoma. xiv+c.120 pp. hdl:20.500.12661/4242
tone_statements.quote: Tone is one of the major characteristics of most Bantu languages (Mambwe, 2008). Kirombo has two types of tone, which are high (H) and low (L) tone. In nouns, high and low tones are significant. In Kiseri, for example, the word kutu has two different meanings depending on the tone. This can be proved by the sets of examples below: [1] /kutú:/ 'ear' [2] /kutù/ 'rust' [3] /irá/ 'hold on' [4] /irà/ 'a leaf' [5] /ikandá/ 'kneading' [6] /ikandà/ 'skin (of fruit)/ shell' ... From the findings of this study, the four studied dialects of Kirombo are tonal dialects. This is because a word can have two different meanings based on the syllable with the high tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.1.1.3 'Suprasegmental features', 4.1.1.3.1 'Tone', pp. 52-53 (examples [1]-[6]); abstract p. vi; summary ch. 5
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H vs L, lexically contrastive (minimal pairs by H placement) in all four Rombo dialects; no further analysis.

tone_statements.citation: Mramba, Peter T. 2020. Ruwaza za Toni katika Vitenzi Visoukomo Changamani vya Kirombo [Tone patterns in complex non-finite verbs of Kirombo]. East African Journal of Swahili Studies (Jarida la Afrika Mashariki la Masomo ya Kiswahili) 2(2): 168-196. EANSO. doi:10.37284/eajss.2.2.242
tone_statements.quote: Kulingana na matokeo ya tafiti hizo na ikizingatiwa kwamba Kirombo ni miongoni mwa jamii lugha za Kichaga, Kirombo pia kina toni ingawa haikuelezwa ruwaza yake ya utokeaji ikoje hususani kwa vitenzi visoukomo changamani. ... Aidha, Kirombo kinadhihirisha wazi kina toni kulingana na ruwaza za maneno yake ambayo kiothografia huonekana sawa ilhali wazawa wa lugha hiyo wanapoyatumia katika mazungumzo yao huchomoza maana tofauti.
tone_statements.translation: Given the results of those studies, and considering that Kirombo is one of the Chaga speech communities, Kirombo too has tone, although how its patterns are realised had not been described, especially for complex non-finite verbs. ... Moreover, Kirombo clearly shows that it has tone through the patterns of its words, which look identical orthographically yet yield different meanings when native speakers use them in conversation.
tone_statements.locator: p. 170 (tone status of Kirombo, minimal pairs ex. 1); p. 172 (two tones J/C = H/L, marking); pp. 173-193 derivations; Hitimisho p. 194
tone_statements.summary: Privative /H/ vs default L on the syllable; lexical H placement contrastive; verb-infinitive surface patterns derived by H spread/shift/copy and OM-triggered stem-H deletion.

tone.translation: Moreover, Kirombo clearly shows that it has tone, judging from word patterns that look identical in spelling but yield different meanings when native speakers use them in speech. Consider example (1): a) ílya 'to eat' / ilyá 'to refuse'; b) íla 'to sleep' / ilá 'to call'. Thus in 1(a) we see: when the high tone appears on the first syllable of the word the meaning is 'eat', and the meaning changes to 'refuse' when the tone appears on the second syllable of the word.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Lexical tone, two tones H (J) vs L (C) with H treated as the underlying marked tone; contrast carried by H placement within the word (minimal pairs, also noun/verb pairs); monosyllabic-stem infinitives/nouns = H prefix + L stem; surface falling tone from glide formation; TBU = syllable; no stress claim.

sources.citation: Julius, A. T. [Julius Alex Tarimo]. 2023. Linguistic variations among dialects of Kirombo. MA (Linguistics) dissertation, The University of Dodoma. xiv+c.120 pp. hdl:20.500.12661/4242
sources.quote: Tone is one of the major characteristics of most Bantu languages (Mambwe, 2008). Kirombo has two types of tone, which are high (H) and low (L) tone. In nouns, high and low tones are significant. In Kiseri, for example, the word kutu has two different meanings depending on the tone. This can be proved by the sets of examples below: [1] /kutú:/ 'ear' [2] /kutù/ 'rust' [3] /irá/ 'hold on' [4] /irà/ 'a leaf' [5] /ikandá/ 'kneading' [6] /ikandà/ 'skin (of fruit)/ shell' ... From the findings of this study, the four studied dialects of Kirombo are tonal dialects. This is because a word can have two different meanings based on the syllable with the high tone.
sources.locator: sec. 4.1.1.3 'Suprasegmental features', 4.1.1.3.1 'Tone', pp. 52-53 (examples [1]-[6]); abstract p. vi; summary ch. 5
sources.note: A Labovian dialect-variation MA (45 speakers, Praat), not a tone analysis, but with a dedicated tone subsection: states Kirombo has two tones, High and Low, that tone is lexically distinctive in nouns, gives H-placement minimal pairs from Kiseri (kutu 'ear' vs 'rust', ira 'hold on' vs 'a leaf', ikanda 'kneading' vs 'skin/shell'), notes the kutu pair exists only in Kiseri, and concludes that all four studied dialects are tonal; abstract and ch. 5 list tone, length and intensity as the main phonological axes of inter-dialect variation; vowel length also contrastive (4.1.1.3.2).
